seo.title: Karmic tail 12 4 19 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 4 19 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Emperor and The Sun. Why a couple that is good at waiting and building finds open joy the hardest.

title: Karmic tail 12-4-19 in compatibility: the happiness a couple hides from the sun
short: Waite gives The Sun three divinatory meanings, and the middle one is "fortunate marriage". In a couple with the karmic tail 12-4-19, this card stands on the main task, the point that shows what the two of them find hard. How did a fortunate marriage become a task? The answer is written in the three cards. The couple enters the task through The Hanged Man: a shared pause and a mutual "not yet". It passes the middle through The Emperor: decisions, rules and a given word. And what it has to learn is The Sun: to be glad out loud, in broad daylight. Such a couple has its happiness. It keeps it hidden.

sections.h2: The bower where honeysuckle shut out the sun
paragraphs: Shakespeare wrote Much Ado About Nothing around 1598. He took the story of the slandered bride from Bandello and Ariosto, but the play's second couple, Beatrice and Benedick, he seems to have invented himself: no direct source for them has been found. And it is this second couple that became the heart of the play. Two and a half centuries later Berlioz named his opera after them: Béatrice et Bénédict.

This couple is so close to the 12-4-19 tail that a single speech of the play holds all three of its cards. Hero, Beatrice's cousin, sends her maid to lure Beatrice into the garden so that she will overhear talk about herself:

"And bid her steal into the pleached bower, / Where honeysuckles, ripen'd by the sun, / Forbid the sun to enter, like favourites, / Made proud by princes, that advance their pride / Against that power that bred it."

Hiding to hear what others say about you is The Hanged Man: life in suspension and a view of yourself from someone else's side. Favourites made proud by princes speak the language of The Emperor, of power and order. The sun that is forbidden to enter is the card of the main task. But the mechanism matters more than any of the three cards. The honeysuckle is no enemy of the sun: the sun is what ripened it. What grew in the light keeps the light out, the way a favourite turns against the power that raised him.

That is the secret of the 12-4-19 tail. This couple's pause, its irony, its order all grew out of love — out of how bright and interesting the two of them are together. And they are what bars love's way when it wants to come out into the open. Beatrice and Benedick walk this path in five acts, and they walk it in exactly the order of the cards.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a merry war instead of a confession
paragraphs: The first thing the audience learns about these two is that they share a language. "There is a kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick and her: they never meet but there's a skirmish of wit between them," Beatrice's uncle Leonato warns his guests. Both swear they will never marry. Both mock lovers. Both talk so alike that they seem to be each other's reflection.

This is what The Hanged Man looks like at the entry to the task. This point of a couple's tail is what the two want together: their agreement, their common language. In a 12-4-19 couple the shared wish sounds odd: not to hurry. Not to give in first. Not to name what is between them. Lisovskaya reminds us that the point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. Shakespeare's pair shows exactly that: the language of mockery both protects them and keeps them from each other.

The Hanged Man hangs upside down, and his world is inverted. Hero describes Beatrice in almost those terms: of any man "she would spell him backward" — a fair-faced one should have been her sister, a silent one is "a block moved with none" — "so turns she every man the wrong side out". An inverted gaze is a gift and a trap at once. It notices what others walk past. "I can see a church by daylight," Beatrice boasts of her eyesight. There is one thing such a gaze cannot see: itself.

The two are a mirror here. In the story invented for Benedick's benefit, Beatrice supposedly says of him: "I measure him by my own spirit." The fiction turned out to be the truest line in the play. The same mirror appears in the numbers: in 88.5% of couples with this tail, both partners have The Lovers, 6 and 6, on the personal point "Entry of relationships and the tail". In the "Compatibility of characters" section the site shows this as matching wishes. The two want the same thing, and two identical wishes added together make The Hanged Man — a pause.

What brings such a couple out of suspension? In Shakespeare, a plot by friends. Prince Don Pedro takes it upon himself to match the two mockers and promises: "we are the only love-gods." Benedick hides in the arbour and hears his friends pity Beatrice, who is supposedly pining for him. Beatrice hides in the honeysuckle and hears the same about him. Each learns about themselves from outside, through other people's eyes — the very reversed perspective of The Hanged Man. Describing the twelfth energy in a couple, Lisovskaya notes that such couples take a long time to enter a relationship, and that something from outside often pushes them towards marriage.

In life this is recognisable at once. Two people spend years in the status of "no idea what we are". At other people's weddings they compete in jokes about weddings. After a quarrel each waits for the other to text first — and nobody does. Friends have long been saying "but you're a couple", and both laugh. And in the end something from outside tips the decision: a move, a parent's question, someone else's wedding, a stray remark from a mutual friend.

Beatrice speaks the formula of this entry at the least fitting moment, in a church: "I confess nothing, nor I deny nothing." Neither yes nor no — a suspended answer. It holds all the strength of The Hanged Man: the pause gives two people time to study each other without haste or illusion. And all its danger: a pause can last for years.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: "Enough" — the day the jokes ran out
paragraphs: The suspension ends not in a confession but in a disaster. Midway through the play, the wedding of Hero and Claudio collapses at the altar: on a false accusation, the groom shames the bride in front of everyone. Her father curses her, the friar proposes announcing that she is dead. Beatrice and Benedick are left alone in the empty church — and for the first time they speak in earnest.

"I do love nothing in the world so well as you: is not that strange?" Benedick asks. A minute later he is ready for anything: "Come, bid me do any thing for thee." — "Kill Claudio." — "Ha! not for the wide world." Claudio is his friend and comrade in arms. Beatrice wants a deed, not words: "manhood is melted into courtesies, valour into compliment, and men are only turned into tongue."

This is where The Emperor rises in the play. Before deciding, Benedick asks a single question: "Think you in your soul the Count Claudio hath wronged Hero?" — "Yea, as sure as I have a thought or a soul." — "Enough, I am engaged; I will challenge him." Waite's divinatory list for The Emperor includes "aid, reason, conviction; also authority and will". In Tatiana Shchepkina-Kupernik's Russian translation Beatrice's answer even uses that very word, ubezhdenie — conviction. And at his next meeting with Claudio, Benedick says something his speech has never held before: "You are a villain; I jest not."

The middle of the task is how a couple travels from the wish to the main task — what it does and what it goes through. Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own; this is our reading. In a 12-4-19 couple the road runs through The Emperor: from words to decisions. The jokes end and an alliance begins. For the first time the two stand together against the world — and discover that this is what they do best.

Curiously, Beatrice has already turned down a ready-made Emperor once. In the second act the prince half-jokingly offers himself as her husband: "No, my lord, unless I might have another for working-days: your grace is too costly to wear every day." She has no use for a crown. A 12-4-19 couple doesn't borrow its order either — not from parents, not from other people's models. It builds its own Emperor, and builds it precisely for working days: the household, money, schedules, who is responsible for what.

From outside, the middle of such a couple looks solid. A joint account and a joint plan. Rules agreed once and for all: no quarrels in front of guests, big things decided together, no calling each other at work. In a crisis these two are magnificent: touch one, and the other is already at their side. Love here speaks in deeds — a fixed tap, a pickup at the airport at three in the morning, a debt paid off on time.

Reliability has a reverse side. Benedick proves his love by going off to fight his friend. A couple in the middle of the task risks proving its love the same way — by execution: doing instead of saying. Rules invented in a hard hour stay on after the hour has passed and start to get in the way. Decisions are made for both, and feelings go unspoken: "it goes without saying". Among the tasks of a couple with The Emperor, Lisovskaya names both rules that later get in the way and learning to talk about feelings. The second of these tasks will come back — in the main one.

In the Messina of Shakespeare's day a challenge to a duel is "a man's office", as Beatrice herself says. In a 12-4-19 couple the roles are not split by gender: either partner can take on The Emperor, or the two can take turns. And in the play the duel never happens. The truth is uncovered not by the clever people but by the night watch, led by the pompous constable Dogberry. The captured villain Borachio confesses to the prince: "what your wisdoms could not discover, these shallow fools have brought to light." The order the two relied on cannot reach the truth by itself. Light arrives from the side nobody was watching.

The main task is the point a couple's tail is read for. Lisovskaya reads it mostly through the minus: what the two find hard and what they need to learn. In a 12-4-19 couple The Sun stands here, and that is the strangest thing about this tail. Waite's divinatory list for The Sun reads: "Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment." The card of a fortunate marriage turned out to be a task. What this couple needs to learn is not steadfastness or loyalty — the entry and the middle teach those. What it needs to learn is happiness.

The last scene of the play shows how hard that is. The truth is out, Hero is alive, everyone is gathered, the wedding is set. That morning the prince notices that Benedick's face has not a ray in it: "Why, what's the matter, / That you have such a February face, / So full of frost, of storm and cloudiness?" Benedick asks the friar to marry him, and when the ladies unmask he asks Beatrice in front of everyone: "Do not you love me?" — "Why, no; no more than reason." She asks him — and hears the same. The phrase is exact: "no more than reason". Love is capped by reason once again, a word from The Emperor's list. Having come all the way through the middle, the two hide once more behind their familiar common language.

Their hands save them. Claudio produces "a halting sonnet of his own pure brain, fashion'd to Beatrice", and Hero a poem by Beatrice to Benedick, "stolen from her pocket". Each had secretly written to the other and never handed it over. "A miracle! here's our own hands against our hearts," says Benedick. **This couple's sun rose long ago. They were simply keeping it in a pocket.**

Even now the "yes" does not come out straight. "Come, I will have thee; but, by this light, I take thee for pity." — "I would not deny you; but, by this good day, I yield upon great persuasion; and partly to save your life." Both swear by the daylight — and at once hide under a joke the very thing they swear to. Benedick ends it the only way open to him: "Peace! I will stop your mouth" — and kisses her.

This is what the main task looks like in the minus. Not coldness and not disaster, but an inability to say something good without armour. Such a couple "doesn't do anniversaries, that's not us". One partner learns of the other's success from mutual acquaintances and answers with a quip. "I'm happy with him" or "I'm happy with her" is heard by friends, by parents, by anyone — except the partner. At their own celebration the two keep glancing at the clock. One protects the other so carefully that neither worry nor joy can get through. Among the tasks of a couple with The Sun, Lisovskaya names an inability to talk about problems, holding feelings back, and taking credit for the partner's victories.

When Lisovskaya analyses a couple's tail, she notes in brackets which energies each conclusion comes from. Walk 12-4-19 her way and two forks appear. Inflated expectations are a task she lists for both The Hanged Man and The Sun (12 + 19). Shakespeare gave them a voice in Benedick's soliloquy: "Rich she shall be, that's certain; wise, or I'll none; virtuous, or I'll never cheapen her; fair, or I'll never look on her; mild, or come not near me; noble, or not I for an angel; of good discourse, an excellent musician, and her hair shall be of what colour it please God." Demanding "everything at once" keeps the pause going longer than any fear. Talking about feelings is a task she sets for both The Emperor and The Sun (4 + 19). That is why the heart of this tail is not a deed but a sentence.

The play's finale also shows The Sun's strong side. "Since I do purpose to marry, I will think nothing to any purpose that the world can say against it," Benedick declares — the very man who feared mockery more than anything. "A college of wit-crackers cannot flout me out of my humour." And then he does what The Sun in action is: "let's have a dance ere we are married, that we may lighten our own hearts and our wives' heels." The master of the house objects like an Emperor: "We'll have dancing afterward." — "First, of my word; therefore play, music." Joy here doesn't wait for order to be put in place. Benedick even postpones the punishment of the captured villain: "Think not on him till to-morrow." And among the last lines is the sad prince, to whom Benedick calls: "Prince, thou art sad; get thee a wife, get thee a wife." The Emperor stands aside; the couple dances.

sections.h2: What Waite drew: a nimbus, three faces and two children by a wall
paragraphs: The pictures of Waite's deck add a few more clues to the story. The Hanged Man hangs upside down, and around his head, as Waite himself writes, there is a nimbus: "There is a nimbus about the head of the seeming martyr." The light is there already at the entry to the task. Only it is right at the head, and turned upside down along with it. Our reading: the sun of the main task doesn't come to the couple from outside. It is the same light that was there from the start, only set upright.

Benebell Wen notices faces on the three cards of the tail. The Hanged Man's face is "calm and serene". The landscape behind The Emperor speaks of a "stern, severe nature". And the sun itself on The Sun card, she writes, has a face "somehow both stern and serene". The face of the main task is assembled from the faces of the entry and the middle. The couple doesn't have to give up The Emperor's sternness or The Hanged Man's calm. It has to carry both out into the light.

The most unexpected clue is in Waite himself, in his description of the older decks. There, beneath the sun, stands a wall "suggesting an enclosure—as it might be, a walled garden", and in it two children "gambolling, or running hand in hand". The Sun of the old cards is a couple. Waite replaced the two with a single child on a white horse. For a couple's tail the old version is closer: two figures by a garden wall holding hands — like Beatrice and Benedick stepping out of the bower straight into the dance.

And the centre. Every couple with the 12-4-19 tail has Strength, 11, in the centre, in "The atmosphere inside the couple" — in Waite's deck it is numbered VIII. The woman on this card "is closing the jaws of a lion", and Waite connects Strength itself with "the Divine Mystery of Union". Coming out of the bower, Beatrice promises: "Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand." The last thing Benedick does with her in the play is "Peace! I will stop your mouth" and a kiss. **This couple's strength is a gentleness that tames not each other but their own mockery.**

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a light neither of the two carries
paragraphs: A personal chart never has 12-4-19, and the reason is beautiful. For a person with The Sun on the karmic task, the calculation always puts Strength in the centre and The Empress at the entry of the tail: their tail can only be 3-22-19. A 12-4-19 couple has the same Sun on the main task and the same Strength in the centre — in 100% of such couples. But its entry is The Hanged Man and its middle The Emperor, because every point of a couple is the sum of two people's points, not a recalculation. Recalculated by the personal formula, 19 + 11 = 30 → 3, the couple's entry would be The Empress. Our reading: one person reaches the same Sun through abundance and a leap into the unknown, while two reach it through a pause and order.

A couple's main task is the sum of the two personal karmic tasks. In 88.5% of such couples these are Strength and Justice, 11 + 8; in 11.5%, The Wheel of Fortune and The Hermit, 10 + 9. Neither partner has The Sun on their personal karmic task. Running every date since 1900 through the site's engine shows more: in 52% of these couples The Sun appears on none of the fifteen main points of the two personal charts — the points the site uses to compare characters. In 41.3% one partner has it, in 6.7% both do. **Neither of the two brings the light of the main task. It appears only between them.**

Strength and Justice are the very two cards Waite swapped: in his deck Strength is eighth and Justice eleventh. Under either numbering they add up to The Sun. Our reading: one partner's rightness and the other's gentle strength, added together, become light — as long as neither tries to win. Which partner carries which is decided by the birth dates, not by gender or character.

The middle is assembled the same way: in these couples The Emperor's four always comes from 31. In 88.5% that is Temperance and The Star, 14 + 17; in 11.5%, Death and The Moon, 13 + 18. One partner's measure and the other's hope, added together, make order — also our reading.

"The couple's values", the spiritual purpose, is The Lovers in 90.5% of couples with this tail and The Devil in 9.5%. The Lovers is a choice made openly, and that is exactly how the play ends: two people choosing each other in front of everyone. For The Devil, the card of bonds, Shakespeare has a line too. "To bind me, or undo me; one of them," Benedick tells the friar before the wedding.

sections.h2: How the 12-4-19 tail is calculated: an example for 05.11.1975 and 02.01.1976
paragraphs: Every point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices; if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. Take two dates: 05.11.1975 and 02.01.1976. The first partner's personal tail is 6-17-11, the second's is 6-14-8.

The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends. Here the sum of the ends would give the same four, 12 + 19 = 31 → 4, but the middle is counted differently — from the personal middles, 17 + 14. "The couple's values" are not added up from the personal ones either: they are recalculated from the couple's sums and in this example give 6, The Lovers.

After the tail, Lisovskaya advises checking whether the same energies appear at other points. In this example they do. "What to create together" is 12, 11 + 1: The Hanged Man stands there too. "What can spoil it" is 12 again, 6 + 6. And "What fills the union" is 19, 16 + 3: the sun this couple finds hard to let in is the very thing that fills it. This belongs to the example, not to every such couple. The Sun stands on "What fills the union" in 2.9% of couples with the 12-4-19 tail, The Hanged Man on "What to create together" in 10%, and on "What can spoil it" in 8.9%.
A couple's tail is neither a verdict nor a forecast. It shows where the two habitually close the door on the sun. Shakespeare left a few hints for this case.

ul: **Hand over the sonnet in person.** Beatrice's and Benedick's poems to each other were produced by friends, one of them stolen from a pocket. A 12-4-19 couple does well not to wait for its confession to be found: say it first, write it, put it in the other's hand.

**One sentence without armour.** Joking is this couple's native language, and there is no need to give it up. But at least one thing a day is worth saying straight, without irony: "I'm happy with you", "I'm proud of you".

**Dance before the wedding.** Don't postpone joy until everything is settled: the renovation finished, the debt paid off, the holidays lined up. The master of the house wanted dancing after the ceremony; the play chose before.

**Check the rules like the honeysuckle.** Every so often, inspect the order invented in a hard hour: has it shut out the very thing that grew it? A rule that stops joy can be cancelled by both partners together.
**Don't wait for conspirators.** A push from outside works, but a couple that has been waiting years for one can more easily push itself: say out loud what the two of them are to each other.
**Celebrate a partner's win as a shared one.** A partner's success is a reason to dance, not to quip. And not a reason to quietly take the credit.
**Tell a pause from a hiding place.** A pause is for seeing each other properly. A hiding place is for not being seen. The Hanged Man gives the first and takes away the second.

sections.h2: Two fictions that made a truth
paragraphs: Commenting on the play, the Russian Shakespeare scholar A. Smirnov named its main device precisely: "Minus times minus gives plus in algebra; two fictions multiplied together give truth in reality" (our translation). Beatrice and Benedick were lied to — each was told that the other was in love — and a lie multiplied by a lie turned out to be the truth. A couple's tail is read through the minus too. But in 12-4-19 the two partners' minuses, added together, give light: this couple's Sun is assembled from what each of them, separately, had as something else entirely. It is already there. All that is left is to stop keeping it in a pocket.

ul: **12, The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** The shared wish the couple starts from: no hurry, no surrendering first, looking at love upside down. In the reading, The Hanged Man appears twice for such a couple — also as the "Common language", because it is the same point.
**4, The Emperor — middle of the task.** How the two travel the road: from a quip to a decision, from words to a deed. The order that protects the union — and the same order that can dry it out.
**19, The Sun — main task.** Learning something simple: speaking about feelings without irony, celebrating, and not keeping in a pocket what was written long ago.

intro: The triple 12-4-19 exists only in a couple's matrix; a personal chart never has it. Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail its karmic program, so the "12 4 19 program" in the destiny matrix is this same tail. It occurs in roughly one couple in 8,416, or 0.012%: 96th of the 97 possible couple tails. Only 18-21-3 is rarer.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 12-4-19 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which the entry to the task is The Hanged Man, the middle is The Emperor and the main task is The Sun. The two enter the relationship through a pause and a mutual "not yet", travel the road through decisions and rules, and what they have to learn is open joy: speaking about feelings directly and not hiding the happiness that is already there.

faq.q: Can 12-4-19 appear in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. A person with The Sun on the karmic task always has Strength in the centre and The Empress at the entry of the tail, so their tail can only be 3-22-19. The triple 12-4-19 appears only in a couple's matrix, where every point is the sum of two people's points.

faq.q: What is the 12 4 19 program in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: The same thing as the couple's karmic tail 12-4-19. Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail its karmic program: tasks that show mostly in the minus, though they can appear in the plus as well. This triple has no separate "program" of its own.

faq.q: Is the 12-4-19 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A tail shows tasks, not fate, and predicts nothing. The difficulty of 12-4-19 is an unusual one: what the couple lacks is not feelings but the ability to show them. The strength of these two is reliability and solidarity in hard times; the task is to allow themselves joy in broad daylight.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 4 if the partners have 17 and 14 there?
faq.a: Because a couple's points are added together: 17 + 14 = 31, and 31 folds into 3 + 1 = 4. The couple's middle is taken from the two people's personal middles, not recalculated from the ends of the couple's tail.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 4 and 19 cannot stand at the entry, and a search of all dates finds 12-19-4 in no couple at all. These three numbers form only 12-4-19.

unit.meaning: Your task is not to hide the happiness you already have: talk about feelings directly and be glad without waiting for order.
